description: "Shayad," the lead single of Love Aaj Kal, was conceived by Pritam as "an ode to young love," aiming to recapture the timeless quality of the 2009 original's soundtrack. Arijit Singh's gentle, slightly wistful delivery carries an estimated C minor melody at a slow ~72 BPM in 4/4, with the arrangement built around understated piano and warm strings that bloom gradually rather than dramatically. Irshad Kamil's lyrics capture the tentative, uncertain hope of new romance — the "perhaps" of the title. The mood is soft, nostalgic, and tender, deliberately evoking the innocence of first love, and the song's popularity led to multiple reprise versions across the rest of the soundtrack.

"Haan Main Galat" injects youthful, rebellious energy into the soundtrack, with Pritam describing it as deliberately "light and exciting" to reflect a generation refusing to be reshaped by social expectations. Arijit Singh and Shashwat Singh's energetic vocal interplay rides an estimated E minor groove at a brisk ~118 BPM in 4/4, sampling elements from the original 2009 film's "Twist" (itself sampled from the classic Nagin theme), giving the track a playful retro-modern hybrid texture. Irshad Kamil's lyrics embrace being unapologetically "wrong" by conventional standards. The mood is defiant and danceable, offering a sharp tonal contrast to the album's softer ballads.

"Mehrama" is the soundtrack's emotional gut-punch, an aching breakup duet that earned both Darshan Raval and Antara Mitra Filmfare nominations for their performances. Estimated in D minor at a slow, mournful ~68 BPM in 4/4, Pritam's arrangement leans into sparse piano and weeping strings, letting the two vocalists' contrasting textures — Raval's youthful ache against Mitra's more seasoned sorrow — carry the weight of separation. Irshad Kamil's lyrics, also Filmfare-nominated, plead for mercy from heartbreak itself. The mood is devastating and intimate, widely cited by critics as one of the standout tracks of the entire soundtrack.

"Aur Tanha" reunites Pritam with KK — who'd sung "Main Kya Hoon" in the 2009 original — for an atmospheric, rock-flavored number that critics singled out as evoking memories of Life in a... Metro. Estimated in B minor at a moderate ~94 BPM in 4/4, the arrangement features prominent electric guitar, gospel-choir-style backing vocals, and a slow-burning, almost cinematic build. Irshad Kamil's lyrics dwell on growing more alone the more someone is present but unreachable. The mood is pensive and quietly intense, with KK's ageless, textured voice — described by reviewers as never sounding dated — anchoring one of the album's most acclaimed tracks.

"Parmeshwara" closes out Love Aaj Kal's more experimental side, led entirely by rapper Raftaar in a sharp departure from the album's melodic balladry. Estimated in A minor at an aggressive ~140 BPM in 4/4, Pritam builds a beat-driven, bass-heavy production with minimal melodic ornamentation, letting Raftaar's rapid-fire flow carry the track's satirical, confrontational energy. Irshad Kamil's lyrics critique social hypocrisy and performative relationships with biting sarcasm. The mood is brash and cynical, intentionally jarring against the soundtrack's romantic core — Pritam and Imtiaz Ali's way of representing the more cutting, disillusioned side of modern dating culture.

"Dhak Dhak" brings an outlandish, chorus-driven energy to the soundtrack, with Nikhita Gandhi and Akasa Singh's spirited vocals riding a folk-flavored arrangement that reviewers compared to the carnival energy of Jagga Jasoos's "Mombaka." Estimated in F major at a lively ~108 BPM in 4/4, Pritam layers percussive folk rhythms with a big, communal chorus structure, giving the track a celebratory, almost theatrical quality distinct from the rest of the soundscape. Irshad Kamil's lyrics capture a fluttering, excited heartbeat ("dhak dhak") in the throes of attraction. The mood is bright and exuberant, offering a deliberately quirky, crowd-pleasing counterpoint to the album's more introspective tracks.

"Yeh Dooriyan" reprises the title and emotional spirit of Mohit Chauhan's beloved song from the original 2009 Love Aaj Kal, with a newly composed melody for the sequel. Estimated in A minor at a measured ~76 BPM in 4/4, Pritam's arrangement keeps Chauhan's signature warm, slightly raspy vocal tone front and center over restrained acoustic and string textures. Irshad Kamil's lyrics meditate on the strange paradox of distance bringing two people closer emotionally even as they stay physically apart. The mood is reflective and gently sorrowful, functioning as a nostalgic callback for fans of the original while standing as its own distinct composition within the new soundtrack.

The reprise of "Shayad," used as the post-interval film variant per the movie's own credits, hands the soundtrack's central love theme to Jubin Nautiyal's smoother, more melodically embellished voice. The underlying composition retains its estimated C minor key and gentle ~74 BPM tempo in 4/4, with Pritam's piano-and-strings arrangement carried over from the Arijit Singh original. Irshad Kamil's lyrics about tentative, hopeful new love remain the emotional anchor. Nautiyal's interpretation brings a slightly more polished, radio-ready quality compared to Singh's rawer original take, offering a contrasting register for the same melody as the film's narrative moves into its second half.

"Aabaad Barbaad," Ludo's lead single and the soundtrack's biggest hit (ranked India Today's #1 Bollywood song of 2020), captures Arijit Singh at his most emotionally unrestrained. Estimated in D minor at ~80 BPM in 4/4, Pritam's arrangement builds from a hushed, intimate opening into a soaring, anthemic chorus, mirroring the lyric's central tension between being "ruined" or "made whole" by love. Sandeep Shrivastava's lyrics capture devotion so total it becomes almost self-destructive. The mood is raw and consuming, picturized on Aditya Roy Kapur and Sanya Malhotra's segment of the film's multi-narrative structure — widely considered a defining Pritam-Arijit collaboration of the era.

"Hardum Humdum" has an unusual backstory — Pritam originally composed the tune for a planned Life in a... Metro sequel that never materialized, before Anurag Basu repurposed it for Ludo years later (the actual Metro sequel, Metro... In Dino, eventually arrived in 2025). Estimated in F major at a warm ~86 BPM in 4/4, Arijit Singh's tender vocal carries Sayeed Quadri's vow of eternal companionship over a gentle, montage-style arrangement that binds together three of the film's narrative threads. The mood is comforting and devotional, functioning less as a standalone romantic number and more as a connective emotional thread woven through Ludo's interlocking storylines.

"Meri Tum Ho" was picturized on Abhishek Bachchan's segment of Ludo, showcasing a different, more weathered shade of devotion compared to the film's younger couples. Jubin Nautiyal and Ash King's blended vocals ride an estimated G major melody at a steady ~90 BPM in 4/4, with Pritam's arrangement favoring warm acoustic textures and a simple, hummable structure that became one of the soundtrack's three charted hit singles. Sandeep Shrivastava and Shloke Lal's lyrics express unwavering possessive devotion ("you are mine"). The mood is sincere and tender, fitting the older, more grounded romantic arc within the film's ensemble structure.

"Dil Julaha" ("the heart, a weaver") brings celebrated lyricist Swanand Kirkire's poetic, metaphor-rich writing to Ludo's soundtrack, with Darshan Raval's earnest, youthful voice carrying the song's central image of the heart weaving itself around someone. Estimated in C major at a relaxed ~84 BPM in 4/4, Pritam's arrangement keeps things simple and melodic, in line with his and director Anurag Basu's stated goal of crafting songs that offer "a break from the edginess" of the film's chaotic, multi-narrative plot. The mood is warm and unhurried, offering one of the soundtrack's gentler, more contemplative moments amid the film's darker crime-comedy elements.

"Tumse Bhi Zyada" sets the emotionally raw tone of Tadap, with Arijit Singh's pained, high-register delivery joined by Pritam's own backing vocals for added textural depth. Estimated in F minor at a slow ~74 BPM in 4/4, the arrangement builds from a sparse piano opening into a fuller, string-laden swell, mirroring the film's themes of obsessive love and betrayal-driven revenge. Irshad Kamil's lyrics express a love that exceeds all reasonable proportion, foreshadowing the destructive intensity at Tadap's narrative core. The mood is anguished and desperate, marking Pritam's continued specialty in crafting opening-title heartbreak anthems for Sajid Nadiadwala-produced romantic dramas, setting emotional stakes before the story's revenge plot fully unfolds.

"Tere Siva Jag Mein" is Tadap's central romantic theme, layering Shilpa Rao and Darshan Raval's contrasting vocal textures with Charan's added vocal presence for a fuller emotional canvas. Estimated in A minor at a measured ~80 BPM in 4/4, Pritam's arrangement leans on warm strings and a steady, devotional rhythm that suggests the all-consuming, near-spiritual nature of the central romance. Irshad Kamil's lyrics declare that nothing in the world exists beyond the beloved. The mood is tender yet weighty, foreshadowing the depth of devotion that later curdles into the film's revenge narrative — the song proved popular enough to be reissued across three additional alternate versions within the same soundtrack.

"Tu Mera Hogaya Hai" showcases Jubin Nautiyal's smooth, melodically rich voice on a tender declaration of belonging and mutual devotion. Estimated in D major at a flowing ~88 BPM in 4/4, Pritam's arrangement favors gentle acoustic and string textures, with a memorable, easily hummable hook line characteristic of his radio-friendly romantic output. Irshad Kamil's lyrics celebrate the simple, joyful certainty of having found one's person. The mood is warm and contented, offering one of the soundtrack's lighter, more hopeful moments before Tadap's narrative pivots toward darker territory — the song's popularity led to its own "Encore" reprise version sung by Javed Ali elsewhere in the album.

"Hoye Ishq Na" injects a harder, more contemporary edge into the Tadap soundtrack, pairing B Praak's powerful, gravelly vocal style with rapper-lyricist Dino James's punchy verses. Estimated in G minor at a driving ~96 BPM in 4/4, Pritam blends rock-leaning guitar textures with rap cadences, a fusion he'd previously explored sparingly, giving the track an urgent, modern edge distinct from the album's more traditional balladry. The dual lyricist credit (Irshad Kamil and Dino James) reflects the hybrid Hindi-rap verse structure. The lyrics warn against falling into love's destructive grip. The mood is intense and cautionary, mirroring the film's darker emotional undercurrents around obsession and consequence.

The "Cafe Edit" of "Tere Siva Jag Mein" strips the soundtrack's central romantic theme down to Darshan Raval's solo voice over a sparser, more acoustic-leaning arrangement, befitting its cafe/lounge-style branding. Retaining the underlying estimated A minor key but slightly slower at ~78 BPM in 4/4, Pritam pulls back the fuller string orchestration of the original duet, letting an intimate guitar-or-piano-led texture carry the devotional sentiment instead. Irshad Kamil's lyrics about all-consuming devotion remain unchanged. The mood becomes more hushed and personal than the original's grander scale, designed for a more relaxed, ambient listening context rather than the dramatic film-scene placement of the main version.

The reprise of "Tere Siva Jag Mein" offers yet another vocal pairing for the soundtrack's most reused melody, with Mohammed Irfan and Asees Kaur bringing a smoother, more polished duet quality compared to the original's grittier vocal texture. The composition holds to its estimated A minor key and ~80 BPM tempo in 4/4, with Pritam's warm string-led arrangement carried over largely intact. The devotional, all-consuming love expressed in Irshad Kamil's lyrics remains constant across versions. This reprise leans slightly more melodic and radio-friendly than the Shilpa Rao-Darshan Raval original, reflecting Pritam's recurring approach across several 2021-22 soundtracks of extracting multiple emotional registers from a single strong melody.

The "Encore" version of "Tu Mera Hogaya Hai" reinterprets Jubin Nautiyal's original through Javed Ali's classically trained, more ornamented vocal style, adding subtle melodic flourishes the original kept simpler. The underlying composition retains its estimated D major key and ~88 BPM tempo in 4/4, with Pritam's gentle acoustic-and-string arrangement largely unchanged. Irshad Kamil's lyrics about joyful, certain belonging stay the emotional anchor. Javed Ali's interpretation brings a slightly more traditional, soulful color to the same melody, giving listeners a contrasting take on the song's warmth — part of the soundtrack's broader pattern of offering reprise and alternate versions across its key tracks.

production_house: Reliance Entertainment, Phantom Films, 83 Films Ltd.
description: "Lehra Do" is Pritam's sole contribution to the 83 soundtrack (depicting India's historic 1983 Cricket World Cup win), with Arijit Singh's powerful, rousing vocals carrying a call to national pride and self-belief. Estimated in D major at an energizing ~104 BPM in 4/4, the arrangement builds with marching-style percussion, soaring strings, and a triumphant brass-adjacent synth layer designed for maximum stadium-anthem impact. Kausar Munir's lyrics urge unfurling the flag of defiance and proving one's mettle against the odds. The mood is patriotic, motivational, and grand in scale, fitting the film's underdog-against-the-world narrative about Kapil Dev's team defying expectations to win cricket's biggest prize on the global stage.

"Kaala Jaadu" ("black magic") is the lead single of the psychological thriller Freddy, with Arijit Singh and Nikhita Gandhi's vocals capturing the dizzying, almost dangerous pull of infatuation that drives the film's disturbing narrative. Estimated in D minor at a sultry ~100 BPM in 4/4, Pritam layers smooth, groove-driven production with subtle electronic textures and a seductive, slow-building hook, giving the track a moody yet catchy pop sensibility. Irshad Kamil's lyrics describe love as an inescapable spell or sorcery, fitting Freddy's central theme of obsessive desire curdling into something sinister. The mood is alluring and slightly unsettling beneath its surface charm, foreshadowing Kartik Aaryan's character's descent into dangerous obsession within the film's dark psychological framework.

"Tujhse Pyaar Karta Hoon" deepens Freddy's romantic-obsessive undertone, with Raghav Chaitanya's emotionally charged, slightly desperate vocal delivery underscoring devotion that borders on consuming. Estimated in A minor at a measured ~84 BPM in 4/4, Pritam builds a moody, atmospheric arrangement with restrained piano and subtle string layers that swell at key emotional points, mirroring the protagonist's intensifying fixation. Irshad Kamil's lyrics speak of total surrender to love, asking to be consumed entirely by the beloved. The mood is intimate yet quietly unsettling, fitting the film's slow unraveling of a seemingly gentle man's psyche — music that sounds romantic on the surface but carries an undertone of obsession once understood within the film's twist-laden context.

"Tum Jo Milo" offers a gentler, more conventionally tender moment within Freddy's unsettling soundtrack, with Abhijeet Srivastava's warm, sincere vocal delivery describing the simple joy of finding someone who feels like home. Estimated in C major at a relaxed ~88 BPM in 4/4, Pritam keeps the arrangement soft and melodic — light piano, warm strings, and an uncomplicated romantic hook — deliberately contrasting with the album's darker undercurrents elsewhere. Irshad Kamil's lyrics express straightforward gratitude and comfort in companionship. The mood is sincere and soothing on its own terms, functioning within the film as the protagonist's genuine, perhaps naive, perspective on love before the story's darker psychological layers fully surface.

production_house: Aamir Khan Productions, Viacom18 Studios, Paramount Pictures
description: "Kahani," described by its own promotional material as "the soul of Laal Singh Chaddha," is a whimsical waltz built around accordion and plucked strings, evoking the European, fairy-tale-tinged sound Pritam pioneered in Barfi!. Mohan Kannan's earnest, slightly untrained-sounding vocal delivery was deliberately chosen over more polished singers for its endearing sincerity. Estimated in G major at a gentle ~92 BPM in a lilting 3/4 waltz time, the song's innocent, storybook melody mirrors the film's central metaphor of life as an unpredictable tale narrated to strangers. Amitabh Bhattacharya's reflective lyrics use a floating feather as imagery (a direct nod to source material Forrest Gump). The mood is childlike, warm, and nostalgically bittersweet.

production_house: Aamir Khan Productions, Viacom18 Studios, Paramount Pictures
description: "Main Ki Karaan?" ("what should I do?") captures the giddy intoxication of infatuation through Sonu Nigam's seasoned, expressive voice paired with Romy's fresh, energetic delivery. Estimated in D major at a breezy ~110 BPM in 4/4, Pritam infuses the track with light Punjabi folk-pop instrumentation — likely tumbi-style plucked textures and upbeat percussion — giving it a playful, regional flavor distinct from the album's more orchestral pieces. Amitabh Bhattacharya's lyrics portray bewildered, helpless love. The mood is light, charming, and youthfully restless, capturing the protagonist's growing romantic feelings during an earlier chapter of his life story, before the narrative moves toward its more dramatic, war-torn passages.

production_house: Aamir Khan Productions, Viacom18 Studios, Paramount Pictures
description: "Phir Na Aisi Raat Aayegi" is a quietly devastating ballad carried by Arijit Singh's restrained, aching vocal performance, mourning a singular night or moment that can never be recaptured. Estimated in B minor at a slow ~70 BPM in 4/4, Pritam keeps the arrangement spare — led by piano with subtle textural layers from additional keys — letting silence and space do as much emotional work as the melody itself. Amitabh Bhattacharya's lyrics dwell on irretrievable loss and longing for a vanished past. The mood is deeply melancholic and reflective, marking one of the soundtrack's most purely emotional moments, tied to the protagonist's grief and yearning across the film's decades-spanning, bittersweet narrative.

singers: Arijit Singh; Shadab Faridi; Altamash Faridi
production_house: Aamir Khan Productions, Viacom18 Studios, Paramount Pictures
description: "Tur Kalleyan" ("walk alone") draws on Sufi-folk devotional tradition, with Arijit Singh joined by qawwali-trained vocalists Shadab and Altamash Faridi to create a song about healing through inner reflection rather than companionship. Estimated in C minor at a measured ~76 BPM in 4/4, Pritam blends traditional qawwali-style group vocals and hand percussion with his own contemporary melodic sensibility, giving the track spiritual weight. Amitabh Bhattacharya's lyrics counsel walking one's own path and finding strength within after heartbreak. Critics singled this out alongside "Kahani" as capturing the film's essence. The mood is meditative, resilient, and quietly uplifting — depicting emotional healing rather than romantic resolution.

production_house: Aamir Khan Productions, Viacom18 Studios, Paramount Pictures
description: This alternate rendition of "Kahani" hands the storybook waltz to Sonu Nigam's more technically polished, accomplished voice, complete with an additional verse not present in Mohan Kannan's original version. The underlying composition retains its estimated G major key and gentle ~92 BPM tempo in 3/4 waltz time, with the same accordion-and-strings arrangement giving it the same European, fairy-tale charm. While reviewers noted Nigam's version is vocally superior, many found Kannan's earnest, slightly imperfect delivery on the original more emotionally endearing for the character. The mood remains warm, nostalgic, and gently bittersweet, offering an interesting study in how the same Pritam-Bhattacharya composition shifts in feeling depending entirely on vocal interpretation.

production_house: Aamir Khan Productions, Viacom18 Studios, Paramount Pictures
description: "Tere Hawaale," the film's closing song and reportedly Pritam's personal favorite composition for the project, was deliberately stripped of lush orchestration at Aamir Khan's insistence, leaving Arijit Singh's flat, unadorned delivery to carry the song's quiet power. Estimated in A major at ~82 BPM in 4/4, the arrangement draws on gurbani musical phrasing inspired by Punjabi wedding traditions, with Shilpa Rao added later in a lower octave since the melody was never originally written for a female voice. Amitabh Bhattacharya's lyrics, written from the protagonist's perspective as he marries Rupa, speak of total surrender to love and fate. The mood is humble, devotional, and quietly profound — the soundtrack's gentle emotional resolution.

"Leke Prabhu Ka Naam" marked Arijit Singh's first-ever vocal for a Salman Khan film, ending a near-decade-long rift between the two following a 2014 awards-night dispute. Pritam crafts an Arabic-tinged dance number, estimated in D minor at a propulsive ~120 BPM in 4/4, built on Middle Eastern percussion patterns, swirling string flourishes, and a chant-like hook reminiscent of the YRF Spy Universe's established Pathaan-style sonic palette. Amitabh Bhattacharya's lyrics invoke divine blessing while celebrating triumphant romance, with Nikhita Gandhi's vocals adding melodic contrast to Arijit's lead. The mood is grand, celebratory, and exotic, designed for a lavish set-piece song sequence showcasing Salman Khan and Katrina Kaif's chemistry on a big international budget canvas.

"Ruaan" is Tiger 3's tender romantic centerpiece, with Arijit Singh delivering a soulful, restrained vocal performance written by longtime YRF collaborator Irshad Kamil. Estimated in F minor at a slow ~78 BPM in 4/4, Pritam's arrangement leans into piano and lush, cinematic strings that build gradually, echoing the grand-scale romantic balladry he's previously brought to the spy-universe's love theme tradition (in the vein of earlier franchise tracks). Kamil's lyrics speak of an unbreakable, soul-deep bond between two people across time and danger. The mood is intimate and emotionally rich, intended to underscore the enduring love story between Tiger and Zoya — the franchise's central couple — amid the high-stakes espionage plot surrounding them.

production_house: T-Series Films, Bhadrakali Pictures, Cine1 Studios
description: "Hua Main" was Animal's first single and Pritam's sole contribution to its multi-composer soundtrack — though, notably, he chose to credit the song to his production house JAM8 rather than himself personally. Estimated in E minor at a moderate ~98 BPM in 4/4, the track is built around a clap-driven beat and a wailing guitar riff that reviewers singled out as distinctly Pritam, reflecting his self-described love of rock music; he also lent his own voice alongside Raghav Chaitanya's lead. Manoj Muntashir's lyrics capture intense, all-consuming first love. The mood is passionate and raw, scoring the intimate romantic chemistry between Ranbir Kapoor and Rashmika Mandanna's characters early in the film's sprawling, violence-laced narrative.

The title track of Merry Christmas sets a smoky, retro-noir mood befitting Sriram Raghavan's stylish thriller, with Ash King's smooth, lounge-jazz vocal delivery anchoring the track. Estimated in A minor at a relaxed ~84 BPM in 4/4, Pritam leans on muted trumpet-style synths, soft brushed percussion, and a slow-swing rhythm reminiscent of vintage Bombay noir soundtracks — a deliberate homage to old-world Hindi cinema scoring. Varun Grover's lyrics evoke a mysterious, atmospheric Christmas Eve setting rather than festive cheer. The mood is sultry, suspenseful, and cinematic, perfectly mirroring the film's one-night, slow-burn mystery narrative between Katrina Kaif and Vijay Sethupathi's characters.

"Nazar Teri Toofan" carries forward the soundtrack's smoky, atmospheric noir-lounge identity, with Papon's warm, textured voice describing a gaze as powerful and overwhelming as a storm. Estimated in D minor at a measured ~90 BPM in 4/4, Pritam's arrangement favors understated keys, soft brass-like synth textures, and a steady, sultry rhythm that mirrors the film's slow-burn tension. Varun Grover's poetic lyrics frame attraction as something dangerous and disorienting, fitting the mystery-thriller's central romantic intrigue. The mood is hushed, seductive, and slightly ominous — music that feels like it's playing in the background of a dimly-lit 1960s-inspired Bombay nightclub, reinforcing the film's vintage suspense aesthetic.

"Raat Akeli Thi" pairs Arijit Singh's emotive baritone with Antara Mitra's atmospheric vocal textures in one of the soundtrack's most pivotal songs, its title ("the night was alone") directly evoking the film's central premise. Estimated in F minor at a slow ~76 BPM in 4/4, Pritam builds a brooding, minor-key arrangement layering piano, soft strings, and a slow-burning rhythm section that mirrors mounting tension. Varun Grover's lyrics speak of a fateful, solitary night that changes everything. The mood is dark, intimate, and suspenseful, functioning almost as a narrative thread tying the thriller's central twist to its music — heartbreak and danger intertwined in classic Sriram Raghavan fashion.

"Dil Ki Mez" lightens the soundtrack's noir-heavy mood with Shalmali Kholgade's playful, expressive vocals over a charming retro-pop arrangement. Estimated in C major at a breezy ~96 BPM in 4/4, Pritam blends light percussion, vintage-toned keys, and a catchy melodic hook that recalls classic Hindi film pop from decades past, fitting the period-tinged visual world Raghavan favors. Varun Grover's lyrics use the metaphor of a "table of the heart" to describe budding affection and flirtation. The mood is warm, whimsical, and gently romantic — a tonal breather amid the album's brooding, suspense-laced tracks, offering insight into a lighter emotional dimension of the story's central relationship.

singers: Arijit Singh; Nakash Aziz; Dev Negi
description: "Satyanaas" is a high-energy, comic folk-pop number that injects mischievous humor into Chandu Champion's otherwise inspirational sports-drama narrative. Arijit Singh, Nakash Aziz, and Dev Negi trade cheeky verses over an estimated brisk ~138 BPM groove in D major and 4/4, with Pritam layering punchy dhol-style percussion, brass-flavored synth stabs, and a sing-along chorus built for group choreography. Amitabh Bhattacharya's playful, mischievous lyrics describe romantic complications between neighbors with comic exaggeration ("satyanaas" meaning "ruin" used humorously). The mood is boisterous and lighthearted, providing comic relief and village-life texture early in the film before its narrative turns toward Murlikant Petkar's grueling real-life journey.

"Tu Hai Champion" is the soundtrack's central motivational anthem, built to underscore Murlikant Petkar's against-all-odds journey toward becoming India's first Paralympic gold medalist. Arijit Singh and Amit Mishra's powerful, layered vocals ride an estimated driving ~118 BPM groove in G major and 4/4, with Pritam building from a restrained opening into a soaring, drum-and-string-heavy crescendo by the final chorus — a hallmark of his sports-anthem compositions. IP Singh's lyrics directly affirm inner championship and resilience regardless of circumstance. The mood is uplifting, triumphant, and cinematic, designed for training-montage sequences and to function as the film's emotional and thematic rallying cry.

"Sarphira" ("the madly determined one") channels raw, rebellious energy through Sreerama Chandra's powerful rock-edged vocals, capturing the protagonist's relentless, almost reckless determination. Estimated in E minor at a driving ~128 BPM in 4/4, Pritam builds the track around distorted electric guitar riffs and a propulsive drum pattern, giving it a harder, grittier edge than the soundtrack's other anthemic numbers. Kausar Munir's lyrics celebrate obsessive, unstoppable willpower in pursuit of one's goal. The mood is intense and adrenaline-charged, designed for the film's training and struggle sequences — embodying the single-minded madness required to overcome the physical and bureaucratic obstacles Murlikant Petkar faced on his path to glory.

"Jamoore" brings an earthy, folk-rooted texture to the Chandu Champion soundtrack, with Mame Khan's distinctive Rajasthani-folk timbre paired against Kailash Waghmare's grounded vocal delivery. Estimated in A minor at a moderate ~110 BPM in 4/4, Pritam layers traditional folk percussion and rustic string instrumentation (likely dholak and ektara-style textures) to evoke rural Indian life. Amitabh Bhattacharya's lyrics use the metaphor of a performer's assistant ("jamoore") to reflect on perseverance and humble beginnings. The mood is grounded, soulful, and culturally specific, anchoring the film's portrayal of Murlikant Petkar's modest village origins before his extraordinary rise through the army and onto the world Paralympic stage.

"Jeet Ka Geet" ("song of victory") is a celebratory triumph anthem featuring Shaan's seasoned, robust vocals, marking the emotional payoff of Murlikant Petkar's hard-fought journey. Estimated in C major at a steady, uplifting ~100 BPM in 4/4, Pritam's arrangement builds with brass-like synth flourishes, full string sections, and a soaring chorus structure characteristic of his victory-themed compositions. Kausar Munir's lyrics directly celebrate hard-won success and vindication after struggle. The mood is jubilant and cathartic, intended to accompany the film's climactic gold-medal moment — functioning as the narrative and musical resolution to the underdog story that the soundtrack's earlier, grittier tracks had been building toward.

song_name: Na Door Hai Na Paas Hai
description: "Na Door Hai Na Paas Hai" offers a gentler, more reflective counterpoint to the soundtrack's louder anthems, with Darshan Raval's soft, youthful voice exploring themes of emotional distance and closeness. Estimated in B-flat major at a relaxed ~82 BPM in 4/4, Pritam keeps the arrangement intimate, built around acoustic guitar and warm string textures that swell gently rather than explosively. Kausar Munir's lyrics ponder the paradox of feeling simultaneously near and far from someone or something deeply important. The mood is tender and contemplative, likely scoring quieter emotional beats in Murlikant's story — perhaps relating to distant family or unfulfilled relationships during his demanding pursuit of athletic greatness.

The "Climax Version" of "Sarphira" reinterprets the soundtrack's rebellious rock anthem through Mohammed Irfan's voice, tailored specifically to underscore the film's climactic moments. The underlying composition retains its estimated E minor tonality and driving ~130 BPM tempo in 4/4, but the arrangement likely intensifies dynamically — heavier guitar distortion and a more urgent rhythmic push — to match a pivotal turning-point scene. Kausar Munir's lyrics about obsessive, unstoppable determination remain the emotional throughline. The mood is even more charged and triumphant than the original version, designed to amplify the emotional stakes of Murlikant Petkar's defining moment of victory or breakthrough within the film's narrative structure.

The Bhool Bhulaiyaa 3 title track reworks Pritam's original 2007 "Hare Ram Hare Ram" hook (sung again by Neeraj Shridhar) into an ambitious global crossover, co-composed with Tanishk Bagchi and featuring international star Pitbull alongside Diljit Dosanjh. Estimated in A minor at a thumping ~124 BPM in 4/4, the track fuses EDM-style production, English verses, and Punjabi-Hindi bilingual energy with the original's iconic Sufi-rock chant. Lyrics by Dhrruv Yogi, Sameer Anjaan, and Pitbull blend romantic infatuation with party-anthem bravado. The mood is maximalist and celebratory — a deliberate large-scale reinvention of a beloved 2007 hook for a horror-comedy franchise aiming squarely at mass commercial spectacle.

"Ami Je Tomar 3.0" updates Pritam's original haunting Bengali-language ballad from the 2007 Bhool Bhulaiyaa, this time co-composed with Amaal Mallik and reinterpreted by Shreya Ghoshal's classically rich, emotive voice. Estimated in D minor at a slow, mournful ~78 BPM in 4/4, the arrangement retains the original's atmospheric, folk-tinged melancholy — likely layering esraj or sarod-like string textures with subtle modern production polish. Sameer Anjaan's lyrics (rooted in the original Bengali theme) speak of devoted, almost eerie longing, tying directly into the Manjulika mythology central to the franchise. The mood is haunting and sorrowful, reinforcing the film's psychological-horror undertones beneath its comedic surface.

"Mere Dholna 3.0" reimagines Pritam's beloved original "Mere Dholna" (sung by KK in the 2007 Bhool Bhulaiyaa) through Sonu Nigam's seasoned, soulful voice, with Amaal Mallik co-producing the updated arrangement. Estimated in C minor at a measured ~80 BPM in 4/4, the recreation preserves the original's emotionally raw melodic core — built on aching strings and a steady, heartbeat-like rhythm — while modernizing the sonic texture for contemporary production standards. Sameer Anjaan's lyrics depict heartbreak and betrayal by those closest to oneself. The mood is deeply melancholic and nostalgic, deliberately designed to evoke fond memories of the original for longtime fans while folding the lament into the new film's supernatural revenge narrative.

The album-opening single "Zamaana Lage" sets Metro... In Dino's tone with a moody, atmospheric alternative-rock arrangement, built around an established Qaisar Ul Jafri ghazal couplet woven into Sandeep Shrivastava's hook. Arijit Singh and Shashwat Singh trade emotionally weary verses over an estimated B minor groove at ~88 BPM in 4/4, with Pritam layering understated electric guitar and electronic textures rather than the traditional harmonium of classic ghazal. The mood is restless and urban — reflecting loneliness within city life — sitting in a meditative, slow-burn zone that echoes the original Life in a... Metro's rock sensibility while sounding distinctly more modern and electronic.

"Dil Ka Kya" is an intimate, minimal acoustic ballad carried solely by Raghav Chaitanya's soft, expressive voice — one of two new Metro Band members alongside Papon. Estimated in D major at a relaxed ~76 BPM in 4/4, Pritam strips the arrangement down to gentle acoustic guitar and light percussion, giving the track an indie, almost unplugged charm distinct from the album's bigger orchestral moments. Anurag Sharma's tender, relatable lyrics ponder the heart's unpredictable, whimsical nature. The overall zone is gentle and reflective — a quiet, conversational love song built for introspective scenes rather than grand romantic gestures, and reportedly a fan favorite among the film's cast.

"Mann Ye Mera" showcases Vishal Mishra's raw, resonant solo voice over Neelesh Misra's introspective, poetic lyricism, a combination known for emotional weight in contemporary Bollywood. Estimated in A minor at ~82 BPM in 4/4, Pritam wraps the composition in earthy acoustic guitar and subtle string orchestration, deliberately understated to let the voice and words carry the song. Described by reviewers as feeling like "a conversation with your own heart," the track sits in a deeply introspective, melancholic zone exploring longing and self-reflection. It's one of the soundtrack's most critically praised tracks, valued for its simplicity and emotional sincerity within the film's mosaic of modern relationship stories.

One of the soundtrack's most acclaimed singles, "Aur Mohabbat Kitni Karoon" finds Arijit Singh delivering pure, unfiltered heartbreak over Pritam's sparse, piano-led arrangement. Estimated in G minor at a slow ~70 BPM in 4/4, the production deliberately stays minimal, letting Arijit's vocal modulation — moving from restrained ache to fuller emotional release — carry the entire weight of the song. Sandeep Shrivastava's lyrics voice unanswered devotion and unfulfilled love, asking how much more one can possibly love. The mood is hushed, vulnerable, and cinematic, representing the soundtrack's emotional peak — described by critics as capturing "love without words."

"Yaad" is a true lyrical and musical gem, adapting classical Urdu poetry by 19th-century poet Momin Khan Momin into a contemporary ghazal. Papon's soulful, classically-tinged rendition rides an estimated slow D minor melody at ~64 BPM in 4/4, with Pritam favoring a soft, semi-traditional arrangement — likely harmonium-adjacent tones blended with modern strings — to honor the poem's old-world gravity while keeping it accessible. The mood is reverent, melancholic, and timeless, evoking longing for a lost or absent love through classical metaphor. It stands apart from the rest of the soundtrack's contemporary pop-rock leanings, anchoring the album's literary, old-world-charm dimension.

"Mausam" plays like a gentle, gradually intensifying breeze, with Arijit Singh's emotive control and tonal purity elevating lyrics that use changing seasons as a metaphor for life's unpredictability. Estimated in E minor at ~74 BPM in 4/4, Pritam's arrangement starts sparse and builds steadily — strings and ambient textures swelling like a memory unfolding in slow motion — a hallmark of his cinematic ballad style. The mood is soothing yet quietly emotional, occupying a reflective, atmospheric zone that mirrors the film's themes of shifting relationships and inevitable change, making it one of the soundtrack's most critically singled-out cinematic moments.

Closing Side A on a celebratory note, "Dhaagena Tinak Dhin" injects energy and flair into an otherwise reflective soundtrack. Sachet Tandon and Akasa Singh's lively vocal chemistry rides an estimated brisk ~132 BPM groove in C major and 4/4, with Pritam blending desi percussion (likely dhol-style beats) with urban pop rhythm and a catchy, repeatable hook line. Mayur Puri's playful lyrics keep the tone light, fun, and danceable. Praised by Bollywood Hungama for its "catchy tune and vibrant visuals," the track functions as a burst of joy and contrast — built for celebratory dance sequences and playlists rather than the album's heavier emotional terrain.

"Qayde Se" reunites the celebrated Pritam-Arijit Singh-Amitabh Bhattacharya combination for a tender, reflective ballad about finding unexpected comfort through heartbreak. Estimated in F minor at ~72 BPM in 4/4, the arrangement favors warm piano and gradually layered strings, allowing Arijit's voice to carry both vulnerability and quiet acceptance. Bhattacharya's lyrics describe pain transforming into a strange sense of relief, and devotion settling "properly" (qayde se) despite past hurt. The mood is intimate, melancholic-but-hopeful, occupying Pritam's reliable space of grand, heartfelt balladry — and proved popular enough to spawn four separate alternate versions across the Side B release.

"Hote Tak" continues the soundtrack's ghazal lineage, this time drawing from the legendary 19th-century poet Mirza Ghalib's verse, reworked with contemporary lines by Sandeep Shrivastava. Papon's soulful, classically-informed voice carries an estimated slow C minor melody at ~66 BPM in 4/4, with Pritam keeping the arrangement modern but restrained — light strings and subtle percussion rather than traditional harmonium-heavy instrumentation. The mood is contemplative and literary, exploring themes of fleeting existence and longing through Ghalib's enduring poetic lens. It exemplifies Pritam's stated approach to this soundtrack: modernizing classical ghazal forms rather than recreating their traditional sound, bridging old-world poetry with current production sensibility.

singers: Papon; Arjun Chandy; Shashwat Singh; Nikhita Gandhi
description: This acapella rendition of "Das Haasil Sau Baaki" strips the song down to pure vocal harmony, with Papon, Arjun Chandy, Shashwat Singh, and Nikhita Gandhi layering voices into intricate, instrument-free textures. Estimated in G major at a moderate ~90 BPM in 4/4, the arrangement relies on call-and-response vocal lines and rhythmic vocal percussion ("para-ra-ree" syllables) instead of conventional instrumentation. Sandeep Shrivastava's lyrics — whose title translates to "ten gained, a hundred remain" — reflect on life's bittersweet incompleteness even amid apparent fulfillment. The mood is warm, communal, and intimate, showcasing Pritam's range by spotlighting vocal arrangement craft over his usual layered instrumental production.

singers: Nikhita Gandhi; Antara Mitra; Shashwat Singh
description: "Ishq Ya Tharak" ("Is it love or just an itch") is the soundtrack's most contemporary, Gen-Z-flavored track, referencing Tinder swipes and modern dating culture in its lyrics. Nikhita Gandhi, Antara Mitra, and Shashwat Singh's breezy, conversational vocals ride an estimated A major groove at ~118 BPM in 4/4, with Pritam opting for a light, bouncy pop production featuring playful percussion and bright synth touches rather than heavy orchestration. Amitabh Bhattacharya's witty lyrics question whether infatuation is genuine love or fleeting attraction. The mood is fun, self-aware, and modern — a deliberate tonal departure into millennial romance territory, performed on-screen prominently by Aditya Roy Kapur.

The "Rewind" version of "Qayde Se" reimagines the original Arijit Singh ballad through Shreya Ghoshal's classically rich, emotive voice, offering a female perspective on the same Amitabh Bhattacharya lyrics about finding strange comfort in heartbreak. The underlying composition retains its estimated F minor key and gentle ~70 BPM tempo in 4/4, with Pritam keeping the core piano-and-strings arrangement largely intact while subtly recoloring it for Ghoshal's vocal texture. The mood remains tender and reflective, but Ghoshal's interpretation brings a softer, more delicate vulnerability than the original. This is one of several alternate takes Pritam built around "Qayde Se," reflecting his tendency to revisit a strong melody from multiple vocal angles.

The "Mood Shift" version of "Zamaana Lage" reworks the album-opening single through Papon's voice, softening the original Arijit Singh-Shashwat Singh duet's restless rock edge into something more contemplative. Retaining the underlying estimated B minor tonality but slowing slightly to around ~80 BPM in 4/4, Pritam dials back the electric guitar presence in favor of a more atmospheric, spacious arrangement that suits Papon's warmer, folk-inflected delivery. Qaisar Ul Jafri and Sandeep Shrivastava's lyrics about urban loneliness remain unchanged, but the new mood leans gentler and more melancholic than urgent. It exemplifies how Pritam used alternate "mood" versions to extract different emotional registers from the same melody.

The "Encore" rendition of "Yaad" transforms Papon's solo classical ghazal into a duet between B Praak and Shilpa Rao, adding a male-female vocal dynamic to Momin Khan Momin's adapted Urdu poetry. The arrangement keeps the same estimated D minor key and slow ~64 BPM pulse in 4/4, with Pritam's traditional-leaning instrumentation intact, but the interplay between two distinct vocal timbres gives the longing expressed in the lyrics a more dialogic, conversational quality — as if two people are remembering the same lost love from different sides. The mood remains reverent and old-world, but the added vocal layer deepens its emotional resonance, making this version feel more intimate as a shared lament.

The "Film Version" of "Qayde Se" is the cut used directly within Metro... In Dino's narrative, sung by Papon in his on-screen role as part of the Metro Band trio alongside Pritam and Raghav Chaitanya. It preserves the song's estimated F minor key and gentle ~72 BPM tempo in 4/4, but trims and restructures the arrangement to fit the film's specific scene timing, likely with a sparser instrumental bed to leave room for dialogue or visual storytelling. Amitabh Bhattacharya's lyrics about heartbreak settling into quiet acceptance remain the emotional anchor. This version underscores Pritam's continuation of the original Metro film's device of band members performing songs diegetically on screen.

The reprise of "Hote Tak" reworks Papon's solo Ghalib-based ghazal into a duet featuring Raghav Chaitanya and Shilpa Rao, adding contrasting vocal textures to the same classical verses. The composition retains its estimated C minor tonality and slow ~68 BPM tempo in 4/4, with Pritam's restrained, modernized ghazal arrangement carried over largely intact. The interplay of Chaitanya's soft, youthful tone against Rao's more seasoned, emotive voice gives the reprise a layered, almost call-and-response intimacy not present in the original solo rendition. The mood remains contemplative and literary, reinforcing the soundtrack's recurring strategy of revisiting key melodies through new vocal pairings to extend their emotional range across the film's narrative.

The reprise of "Aur Mohabbat Kitni Karoon" hands the song's raw heartbreak over to Tulsi Kumar, offering a female-voiced counterpart to Arijit Singh's original rendition. The sparse, piano-led arrangement and estimated G minor key at ~70 BPM in 4/4 remain largely consistent with the original, preserving its hushed, vulnerable intimacy. Sandeep Shrivastava's lyrics about unanswered, unconditional devotion take on a slightly different emotional shade through Kumar's smoother, more delicate vocal tone compared to Arijit's anguished delivery. The mood stays tender and melancholic, functioning as a complementary perspective within the film's narrative — likely tied to a different character's version of the same heartbreak explored in the Side A original.

The original, fully-instrumented version of "Das Haasil Sau Baaki" pairs Raghav Chaitanya and Neeti Mohan in a warm romantic duet, contrasting with its stripped-down acapella sibling. Estimated in G major at a flowing ~92 BPM in 4/4, Pritam builds a fuller arrangement here with light percussion, acoustic and electric guitar textures, and gentle string accents supporting the vocal interplay. Sandeep Shrivastava's lyrics — about gaining much yet still feeling an unfulfilled void — are delivered with more melodic ornamentation than the acapella cut. The mood is wistful yet melodic, occupying a folk-pop romantic space that emphasizes the lyrical theme of life's persistent, bittersweet incompleteness even amid apparent happiness.

Yet another iteration of the soundtrack's most-reused melody, the reprise of "Qayde Se" is carried by Shilpa Rao's textured, soulful voice, joining Arijit Singh, Shreya Ghoshal, and Papon as the fourth vocalist to interpret this central composition. The arrangement holds to its estimated F minor key and gentle ~70 BPM pace in 4/4, with Pritam's piano-and-strings foundation remaining the emotional backbone across every version. Amitabh Bhattacharya's lyrics about finding unexpected comfort within heartbreak stay constant, but Rao's grittier, more world-weary tone gives this reprise a slightly heavier, more resigned emotional color. Collectively, "Qayde Se's" four versions make it the soundtrack's most reworked and thematically central melody.

The lead single of Cocktail 2, "Jab Talak" is a slow-building romantic ballad anchored by Arijit Singh's emotive, slightly raspy vocals, with Akasa and Madhubanti Bagchi adding textured harmonies. Pritam frames the song in an estimated F# minor with a gentle ~90 BPM pulse in straightforward 4/4 time, leaning on his signature piano-and-strings palette layered with soft acoustic guitar and a restrained rhythm section that swells only in the final chorus. Amitabh Bhattacharya's lyrics speak of devotion that outlasts time itself. The mood is intimate and yearning, sitting in that classic Pritam-Imtiaz-style romantic zone — vast, cinematic, but emotionally close, designed to underscore a love story's tender, vulnerable moments rather than its party scenes.

"Mashooqa" is a high-octane club anthem built for the dance floor, with Pritam fusing bass-heavy commercial groove with modern synth-pop and international dance elements, including Italian-language passages reflecting the film's Sicily setting. Estimated to sit around 124 BPM in C minor and 4/4 time, the track features a multi-singer vocal collective — international artist Mahmood, the versatile Raghav Chaitanya, and Ruaa Kayy — trading lines over pulsing synth bass, four-on-the-floor percussion, and bright electronic stabs. Amitabh Bhattacharya's playful, flirtatious lyrics match the track's high-energy, glamorous party zone. It's unmistakably a big-screen production number meant for spectacle, swagger, and ensemble choreography rather than introspection.

"Tujhko" is a tender romantic duet pairing Arijit Singh's warm, emotive delivery with Sunidhi Chauhan's rich, expressive vocals, set to an estimated D major key at a gentle ~80 BPM in 4/4. Pritam builds the arrangement around soft piano chords, warm string pads, and understated acoustic guitar, letting the vocal interplay carry the emotional weight as the song swells gradually toward its hook. Amitabh Bhattacharya's lyrics declare an all-consuming, irreplaceable love — the idea that no one else could ever love this completely. The overall zone is intimate and heartfelt, occupying the soft-focus romantic space typical of Pritam's love-story soundtracks, built to soundtrack a quiet, devotional moment between the film's central couple.

"Vallah" is an upbeat party number featuring Harrdy Sandhu's punchy, rhythmic vocal style alongside Bayanni, set to an estimated brisk ~128 BPM in E minor and 4/4 time. The production leans into thumping electronic percussion, catchy synth hooks, and a chant-like, repeatable refrain designed for instant singalong appeal, consistent with Pritam's knack for crafting radio-friendly dance hooks. Amitabh Bhattacharya's lyrics carry a flirtatious, celebratory energy that fits the song's festive, carefree zone. Positioned as one of the film's pre-release dance singles, the track sits in the high-energy, youthful space meant to soundtrack celebration sequences and promotional choreography rather than the story's quieter emotional beats.

"Bandhu 2.0" is a nostalgic recreation of "Tumhi Ho Bandhu" from the original Cocktail (2012), reuniting Pritam's Sufi-rock sensibility with Neeraj Shridhar's recognizable, gravelly voice and Kavita Seth stepping into the late Shruti Pathak's old part. Estimated in C major at a moderate ~100 BPM and 4/4 time, the arrangement retains the original's folk-rock backbone — acoustic strumming, dholak-style percussion, and a soaring, anthemic chorus — while modernizing the production sheen. Irshad Kamil's lyrics celebrate companionship and belonging, lending the track a warm, communal, celebratory zone. Functioning as an emotional callback for longtime fans of the franchise, it bridges generational nostalgia with the sequel's contemporary sound.

production_house: Balaji Motion Pictures, Cape of Good Films
description: The lead single of Bhooth Bangla, "Ram Ji Aake Bhala Karenge" is a playful, novelty-tinged track that mirrors the film's horror-comedy tone, drawing lyrical comparisons to the classic "Bhooter Raja Dilo Bor." Estimated around G major at a bouncy ~110 BPM in 4/4, Pritam layers folk-flavored percussion, whimsical synth flourishes, and chant-like group vocals from Armaan Malik, Aarvan, and MellowD to create a mock-spooky, sing-along energy. Kumaar's lyrics use ghost imagery and chalisa-style chanting for comic effect rather than genuine scares. The overall zone is theatrical and tongue-in-cheek — eerie instrumentation undercut by playful melody — built to soundtrack the film's haunted-mansion comic set pieces and Ganesh Acharya-choreographed dance sequences.

production_house: Balaji Motion Pictures, Cape of Good Films
description: "Tu Hi Disda" stands out as the soulful romantic core of an otherwise comic horror soundtrack, marking Arijit Singh's notable return to playback after stepping back from singing, reportedly because he felt a deep connection to the composition. Paired with Nikhita Gandhi's emotive voice, the song is estimated to sit in B-flat minor at a slow ~75 BPM in 4/4, built on Pritam's classic combination of piano, swelling strings, and a restrained rhythm section that opens up in the final refrain. Kumaar's lyrics lean tender and devotional. The emotional zone is deeply intimate and yearning, a deliberate tonal contrast to the film's spooky comedy elements, anchoring the love story at the heart of the haunted-mansion narrative.

singers: Vishal Mishra; Nakash Aziz; Antara Mitra
production_house: Balaji Motion Pictures, Cape of Good Films
description: "O Sundari" is an energetic folk-pop number praising the female lead's beauty, with Vishal Mishra and Nakash Aziz's spirited male vocals contrasted against Antara Mitra's melodic responses. Estimated in A major at a lively ~118 BPM in 4/4, Pritam's arrangement uses dhol-driven percussion, bright brass-like synth lines, and a catchy, repetitive hook designed for celebratory choreography. Kumaar's flattering, admiring lyrics keep the tone light and flirtatious. Positioned as a colorful courtship number within the horror-comedy's plot, the song occupies a festive, exuberant zone — closer to a wedding or festival dance sequence than the film's eerie undertones, offering a bright musical break amid the haunted-mansion chaos.

singers: Shreya Ghoshal; Javed Ali; Prithvi Gandharv
production_house: Balaji Motion Pictures, Cape of Good Films
description: "O Ri O Sanwariya" brings a semi-classical, folk-rooted texture to the Bhooth Bangla soundtrack, with Shreya Ghoshal's classically trained voice weaving around Javed Ali's robust delivery and Prithvi Gandharv's earthy timbre. Estimated in D minor at a measured ~85 BPM in 4/4, Pritam draws on traditional instrumentation — likely sarangi or harmonium textures layered with tabla — evoking an old-world, mythological atmosphere fitting the film's Vedic and Mahabharata-inspired horror themes. Yatindra Mishra's poetic lyrics address a dark-complexioned beloved in classical Hindi imagery. The mood is reverent and atmospheric, sitting in a more traditional, soulful zone than the rest of the soundtrack, lending gravitas to the film's mythological backstory.
